extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, literary critics, and psychoanalytic researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, classify, and analyze technical devices used in witticisms (e.g., puns, displacement, nonsense, sophistic faults), and apply reduction to determine which element produces the wit. Emphasis is on theoretical taxonomy and examples for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns (pun)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embraces those jokes which are commonly called 'puns.' These are generally counted as the lowest form of wit, perhaps because they are 'cheapest' and can be formed with the least effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns make the least demands on technique of expression: it is enough if two words for both meanings resemble each other through some slight similarity in structure, in rhythmic consonance, in the community of several vowels, or in some other similar manner. Puns are especially fond of modifying one of the vowels of the word. Anti-pattern: when both meanings use identical words (example Heine's Calcutta/Calcutta roast) the witticism is poor. K. Fischer: 'A pun is a bad play on words, for it does not play with the word as a word, but merely as a sound.' Examples: 'Humbug' (insect made of parts — 'Humbug'); vowel-change puns; simple rhyme/sound resemblances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play on words (word-play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit that 'transfers itself from the sound of the word into the word itself'—a play that makes the word serve as more than mere sound by exploiting its meaning(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from puns (which play on sound only); play on words often uses the manifold application of the same material and may be considered a higher form of sound-wit. Usage and esteem may vary by technical viewpoint. Example: cases where both meanings find expression in the identical word (true play on words) rather than mere sound similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold application / repetition of same material
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique in which the same material (word/phrase) is applied multiple times or in multiple senses to produce wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In plays on words the same material often reaches its height by allowing both meanings to appear; in puns only resemblance suffices. Reduction tests whether manifold application is essential. Example contrast: play on words (both meanings expressed in identical word) vs pun (two similar words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement (psychic-accent shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique whose essential element is the deviation of the trend of thought by displacing the psychic accent to another theme than the original, often realized between statement and answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displacement consists in shifting the stream of thought to a different direction than the one started by the statement; e.g., Heine's 'Oh, he must be older than that' (golden calf → calf→ox), bath joke ('Have you taken a bath?' → misemphasis on 'take'), 'salmon with mayonnaise' (answer deviates from reproach). Displacement is often independent of verbal expression (may survive substitutions so long as sense of answer is adhered to), but sometimes combines with double meaning. It regularly occurs between a statement and an answer and can be retrogressive. Use the reduction method to determine whether displacement is the decisive factor; removal of displacement (or its component) should abolish the wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning (polysemy/homonymy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a word or phrase capable of several interpretations which allows transition from one thought to another and supplies material for wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double meaning may make possible a displacement but is conceptually distinct: in double-meaning wit the word itself contains multiple interpretations (Group II, f). Examples: 'living' meaning 'alive' vs colloquial 'making a living' (schadchen joke); 'take' in 'take a bath' (idiomatic vs literal). Reduction: removing the double meaning (or changing wording) can abolish the wit when the wording is essential. Distinguish 'wit-work' (psychic processes producing wit) from 'understanding-work' (processes by which hearer comprehends multiple meanings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wording dependence (verbal-form dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some witticisms require specific phrasing or wording for the wit to function; changes in wording nullify the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the bath joke hinges on 'Have you taken a bath?' vs wording 'Have you bathed?'; altering wording can destroy the double meaning or displacement. When analyzing, attempt substitution; if wit disappears, the wording was essential. This helps distinguish displacement-wit that depends on wording from displacement independent of wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction method (analytic test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of analysis in which you 'reduce' the joke—alter or remove elements—to see which element is essential to producing the wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction is an 'unfailing way for tangible demonstration' of which technical element generates the wit. Example: remove the expression that allows double meaning or remove the displacement to see if wit survives. Used repeatedly to distinguish double meaning, displacement, nonsense, and other mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement vs Double-meaning differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical distinction: double meaning provides lexical ambiguity allowing a transition of thought; displacement is a structural shift in the stream of thought (a move in the wit-work itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although related (double meaning can enable displacement), they are separate techniques. In displacement-wit the displacement is contained in the production of the wit (the 'wit-work') rather than merely in the listener's understanding. Use reduction to separate them: preserve double-meaning but remove displacement (or vice versa) to test which produces the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense used as a technical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Advancing something apparently absurd or nonsensical which, however, discloses a sense serving to illustrate or represent some other absurdity; nonsense transformed into wit by revealing sense within or using absurdity for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: officer advising Ike to buy a cannon (imitates stupidity to expose it), 'Never to be born would be best for mortal man' / 'hardly one in a hundred thousand has this luck' (appendix exposes original as nonsense), father/daughter screen joke. Nonsense may expose another piece of nonsense or create a startling, puzzling effect. Reduction may expose the underlying sense; nonsense-wit often imitates the target's stupidity to make the target conscious of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization-wit (show-side vs function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticism that appears to be a characterization (a caricature or illustration of a person's traits) but whose 'object' or surface characterization serves a different technical purpose in producing the wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'schadchen' (marriage-broker) who uses double meaning and displacement—what seems like mere characterization is the 'show-side' while the technical mechanism lies deeper. When analyzing, look past surface characterization to the technical device (double meaning, displacement, etc.) that generates the wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistic faulty thinking (fallacious logic used as technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of apparently logical but actually fallacious or sophistical reasoning as a device for wit—presenting errors of thought in a logically facaded form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: customer who returns cake then takes liqueur and claims he owes nothing; marriage-agent who treats faults individually, ignoring their cumulative effect; A's kettle defense (three mutually exclusive assertions). The technique exploits semblance of logic to conceal contradiction; common errors include treating cumulative factors individually, using 'and' where 'either-or' applies, or forming spurious relations by double sense. Reduction/unpacking reveals the faulty premises and dissolves the wit. This category overlaps with 'logic as facade' but specifically highlights sophistic structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal / Means-and-Ends inversion (cynical reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique that inverts the normal means-ends relationship to create a witty or cynical remark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the drunk who 'gives lessons in order to be able to drink' (inversion of means and ends). The wit rests on exposing the perverse prioritization; often depends on expression and may blur into cynicism rather than pure displacement or nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical facade or semblance of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a logical-sounding structure or argument as a façade to present absurdity or faulty reasoning in a way that elicits laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to sophistic faulty thinking; the 'facade' convinces the hearer momentarily of coherence, so the underlying absurdity or contradiction surprises and amuses. Examples include marriage-agent's stepwise neutralizations of faults and the shop-customer's returned-cake logic. Analysis should uncover the hidden contradiction or erroneous combination of premises.
